title: Redwood - Acme Financial: Security & Incident Response Review
summary: High-level review of SOC 2 / ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO integrations, audit logs and KMS integration. Deep dive into incident response, BCDR (RTO/RPO), SLA/uprimes and escalation flows. Agreed next steps: share SOC2/ISO reports, provide IR runbook, schedule tabletop exercise, propose SLA language for pilot.
action_items: Jordan Meyers: Send SOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 cert, and SOC control matrix (due 2025-11-19)
Priya Singh: Share technical runbook for incident response and BCDR, include sample RTO/RPO numbers and playbooks (due 2025-11-20)
Carlos Ruiz: Provide architecture diagram showing VPC, private endpoints, KMS flow, and audit log streaming options (due 2025-11-21)
Lisa Chen / Acme: Confirm acceptable RTO/RPO ranges and proposed pilot SLA targets (due 2025-11-24)
Jordan Meyers: Schedule tabletop incident response exercise w/ Acme stakeholders (tentative week of 2025-11-24)
Maya Holt: Share Redwood's escalation contact matrix and on-call hours for Dedicated/Private customers (due 2025-11-19)
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack (SOC2, ISO certs, pen test summary)
Customer to review runbook and propose RTO/RPO for pilot
Set date for tabletop IR exercise
Draft pilot SLA language and credit terms for review
Confirm data residency options and KMS key ownership model
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-12 16:30 UTC | Duration: ~60m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood Security), Lisa (Acme CISO), Tom (Acme Head of Platform), Rupal (Acme Compliance), Ethan (Acme SRE), Nora (Acme Legal)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. This call is mainly to walk through our security artifacts and then do a focused discussion on incident response and BCDR, the RTO/RPO expectations, and how escalation works. I see Lisa and team on, do you want to kick off with your primary concerns?

[00:18] Lisa: Sure, thanks. High level, Acme's procurement and risk review want to validate SOC 2 and ISO artifacts, understand how RBAC and SSO will integrate with our IdP, and crucially we need comfort on incident response — detection, comms, RTO, RPO. Because we're a financial services firm data residency and key management are big for us.

[00:40] Priya: Totally makes sense. We'll walk through what we can share today and what we provide during pilot. Quick note: for private deployments you can own KMS keys, for dedicated we can integrate with your cloud KMS via customer-managed keys. For hosted there are options for Bring Your Own Key with HSM integrations.

[01:05] Tom: When you say BYOK for hosted, do you mean we hold keys in our cloud KMS and Redwood can call them, or you host the key? We need to avoid key export.

[01:20] Carlos: Right, good question. For the hosted offering we use a customer-key-in-cloud pattern: your KMS holds the key material, Redwood requests encryption/decryption via secure API with limited key access. Keys are never exportable to Redwood. For Private/Dedicated deployments you can run the key in your VPC and we never touch key material. We'll share a diagram.

[01:44] Lisa: OK that helps. Next, audit logs — we need raw access to logs for incident forensics and SOC reporting. What's retention and format?

[01:56] Priya: Audit logs are emitted to configurable sinks. For Dedicated and Private you can push to your SIEM or S3 with lifecycle rules. For hosted we retain logs for 90 days by default, with extended retention add-ons. Logs include request metadata, route, user id mapping, token/usage metrics, and errors. Some of the auto transcribed fields may have noisy names, but we provide structured JSON.

[02:20] Ethan: Are the logs immutable? We require tamper evidence for important events.

[02:26] Maya: Logs are write-once in the pipeline and we support signed delivery to your bucket with object versioning. For higher assurance we can do log hashing and provide manifest files. We'll surface the exact controls in the pack.

[02:45] Rupal: On SSO — we use SAML + SCIM for provisioning. Does Redwood support SCIM for user sync and role mapping?

[02:53] Priya: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported. Role-based access control maps SCIM group attributes to Redwood roles. There are a couple places where attribute names can get fuzzy in the logs (e.g., SAMl sometimes shows up as SAMl in exports) so we'd advise verifying mapping in a test environment.

[03:20] Nora: For compliance we'd like to see the control matrix and who has access to what in your org, plus counsel on separation of duties.

[03:32] Jordan: We'll include the control matrix. Also note our internal access is role-limited; access to customer data and keys is logged and requires approval. Maya, want to add?

[03:42] Maya: Sure — we maintain least-privilege defaults and quarterly access reviews. Privileged operations require 2-person approval in our playbook. We'll include a snapshot of the access review process and the approval workflow.

[04:00] Lisa: Great. Now onto incident response — say there's a partial regional outage impacting inference latency and some KV cache invalidation. What's your detection and response timeline? What's typical RTO/RPO?

[04:16] Priya: We operate a tiered detection system: automated health checks and anomaly detectors, then on-call SREs. For Dedicated customers we have a published RTO target of 30 minutes for critical incidents and an RPO of 1 minute for stateful caches if you're on our recommended replication configuration. For hosted offerings the RTO is similar but depends on the plan; for enterprise we can negotiate stricter SLOs in the contract.

[04:48] Ethan: 1 minute RPO for KV cache — what's the replication topology? Multi-AZ?

[04:53] Carlos: Multi-AZ replication for stateful components is standard in Dedicated. KV cache is replicated synchronously within a region and asynchronously cross-region depending on config. We'll provide exact replication diagrams; RPO depends on replication window and whether you use prefix caching.

[05:12] Lisa: For regulatory purposes we need a documented incident timeline and communication plan — who's notified internally and externally, SLA credit triggers, and what constitutes a P1 vs P2.

[05:25] Jordan: We have standardized incident severity definitions. P1 is system unavailable for >5% of requests or complete outage for an app-critical route — that triggers our 24/7 on-call and executive notify. We will provide the escalation matrix with phone and Slack channels.

[05:41] Priya: I'll note that our escalation includes steps: detect -> mitigate -> contain -> communicate -> recover -> postmortem. For communication we provide initial customer-facing status within 15-30 minutes for P1s, and we post updates every 30 minutes until resolution.

[06:00] Nora: Do you do cross-customer postmortems or are details limited to impacted customers?

[06:08] Maya: Root cause summaries are shared broadly in anonymized form; detailed timelines and debug logs are shared with impacted customers under NDA where necessary. We also publish a public incident report for high-severity incidents with redacted sensitive info.

[06:25] Rupal: About BC/DR tabletop exercises — would Redwood participate or provide runbooks?

[06:32] Jordan: We can run a joint tabletop with your incident commanders and ours. Priya will lead the technical scenario and Maya/sre will do the escalation simulation. We usually run a 2-3 hour session and produce an action log.

[06:48] Lisa: That would be useful. Regarding SLA, what are uptime guarantees and credit calculations?

[06:56] Carlos: Our standard SLA for Dedicated is 99.9% per month for the inference control plane (we can provide a draft SLA). For higher tiers we can offer 99.95% with penalties/credits defined as a percentage of monthly fees prorated by the downtime. We'll draft sample language for the pilot.

[07:15] Ethan: For latency SLOs are those at the 95th percentile or p99? Also, what about burst capacity — if you throttle, what's the fallback?

[07:26] Priya: We typically measure p95 for throughput SLOs and p99 for tail latency where specified. For throttling we have congestion control and fallbacks to compatible model variants. For mission-critical customers, we can allocate reserved capacity plus burst policy to meet peaks.

[07:42] Lisa: On escalation, can we get a single-pane on-call list and 24/7 escalation phone number? We need guaranteed contact path for P1s.

[07:50] Maya: Yes — we'll provide an escalation contact matrix including primary on-call, secondary, engineering leads, and exec on-call. For Dedicated/Private customers we also provide a named CSM and an enterprise support hotline.

[08:03] Tom: Curious about incident detection instrumentation — do you provide tracing hooks and request-level IDs so we can correlate across our logs and Redwood's?

[08:12] Priya: Absolutely. We inject a request-id header and provide trace IDs in logs and the console traces. You can forward those into your APM/SIEM for end-to-end correlation.

[08:25] Lisa: Pen testing — can we run tests or do you publish an allowed tests list? Also VDP?

[08:31] Jordan: We have a vulnerability disclosure program and will share the VDP. For pen tests, we support coordinated testing against dedicated or private environments; for hosted you need to submit a plan and schedule. We'll include the pen test summary from our last third-party assessment.

[08:48] Rupal: About data residency — Acme requires EU data to stay in EU regions and US data in US regions. Does Redwood support regionally segmented storage and processing?

[08:59] Carlos: Yes — our routing and regional placement policies allow you to pin workloads to regions. For Dedicated or Private you can choose the region and controls. We also support data residency controls in hosted with contractual commitments and region-specific endpoints.

[09:16] Ethan: A practical question: in a full cloud region outage, how do you handle failover? Is there automated failover cross-region and what's the RTO?

[09:25] Priya: Cross-region failover is supported but depends on replication config. For synchronous cross-region replication RTO can be under 10 minutes for control plane failover; for asynchronous setups it may be hours. We recommended pilot testing the failover scenario to validate RTO.

[09:42] Lisa: OK. Regarding legal/comms — if there's a security incident affecting regulated data, what's Redwood's breach notification timeline? We need to ensure we can meet our regulatory obligations.

[09:52] Nora: Typically we require notification within 72 hours for certain regs, but internal SLAs may be tighter. What's Redwood's policy?

[10:00] Maya: We commit to notifying customers within 24 hours for incidents affecting confidentiality or integrity of customer data and provide status updates as available. The exact contractual obligation can be negotiated as part of enterprise terms. We'll include notification thresholds in the pack.

[10:15] Jordan: Quick note: our incident response retainer for enterprise customers offers guaranteed SLOs for response and a named incident manager — we can include pricing options in the follow-up.

[10:28] Lisa: Good. Can we see an example postmortem and the timeline of communications?

[10:34] Priya: We'll anonymize a recent postmortem and show the timeline and remediation steps. That usually helps audit teams assess our response posture.

[10:45] Tom: About metrics you provide — do you expose RTO/RPO reports historically? Like past year dashboards?

[10:51] Carlos: We have per-customer incident dashboards and historical uptime metrics. For Dedicated customers we can provide longer retention and more granular telemetry.

[11:05] Rupal: On the question of SLA credits: how are they calculated — minutes of downtime vs monthly fee?

[11:12] Maya: Credits are typically a percentage of the monthly invoice based on the amount of downtime beyond the SLA. We'll draft the formula and examples.

[11:23] Ethan: For the pilot, can you commit to a P1 initial response time SLA? We need to know when engineering will start remediation work.

[11:32] Priya: For pilot we can commit to an initial acknowledgement of P1s within 15 minutes and engineering engagement within 30 minutes. We'll put that in the pilot terms.

[11:44] Lisa: Sounds reasonable. A couple of smaller items — do you have SOC 2 attachments about encryption at rest vs in transit specifics? We need details on cipher suites, TLS versions, and key rotation cadence.

[11:58] Jordan: Yes, those are in the security pack. Short answers: TLS 1.2+ and 1.3 supported, AES-GCM ciphers for data at rest where applicable, key rotation policy is 90 days by default for platform keys; customer-managed keys follow your KMS rotation policy.

[12:16] Nora: Is there a contractual right to audit? Some of our procurement folks want on-site or remote audits.

[12:23] Jordan: For enterprise customers we offer remote audits and in some cases on-site reviews under NDA and scheduling. We'll include the audit process.

[12:34] Lisa: Great. Let's summarize next steps.

[12:38] Jordan: Recap: Redwood will share SOC2/ISO artifacts, control matrix, incident runbook and escalation matrix, architecture diagram for KMS/log flows, and sample postmortem. Acme to confirm RTO/RPO targets and provide available windows for a tabletop exercise. We'll draft pilot SLA language and retainer options.

[12:55] Lisa: Yes. One ask — can you highlight any differences in incident handling between hosted vs dedicated vs private in the doc? We want a clear table.

[13:04] Priya: Absolutely. We'll add a comparison matrix calling out who owns keys, who owns logs, expected RTO/RPO ranges, and communication channels per offering.

[13:16] Tom: Thanks, that helps. Anything else from legal?

[13:20] Nora: No, just ensure the notification windows and audit rights are explicit. We'll review the draft SLA.

[13:27] Jordan: Perfect. We'll follow up with the pack by next week. Thanks everyone.

[13:33] Lisa: Thanks all.

End of recording.
